implementation_notes: `lazy val` is a language feature rather than a library: the Scala specification says the right-hand side is evaluated the first time the value is accessed, and the compiler emits the one-time guard (Scala 2 synchronizes on the enclosing instance, Scala 3 generates a state-machine-based implementation), so the classic holder-and-flag structure disappears entirely. The same mechanism makes a top-level `object` a process-wide lazy singleton: its initializer runs on first access. Because a lazy val is one-shot and cannot be reset, resources that must be closed or re-acquired belong in an explicit holder - an effect such as cats-effect/zio IO.defer, or a Future created on demand - and because the guard is only marked complete after a successful evaluation, a throwing initializer is retried on the next access.
pitfalls: Self-reference deadlocks or yields null: a lazy val whose initializer reads the same lazy val blocks forever under Scala 2's per-instance monitor (or observes an unassigned field), and trait initialization order makes lazy vals in traits a classic trap.

Accessing a lazy val from a superclass constructor evaluates it before the subclass fields exist, so the cached value can be built from defaults - keep constructors free of lazy access (and enable -Xcheckinit in tests).
Thread safety covers creation, not use: the value is published once, but a mutable resource inside it still needs its own protocol for concurrent callers.
A throwing initializer is not cached - the guard completes only on success - so a failing acquisition retries on every access with no backoff or record.
